Get started with nestedscales

Source: vignettes/nestedscales.Rmd
nestedscales.Rmd

nestedscales provides a discrete representation of a data dimension at several resolutions and the operations that move data between them. This vignette introduces the representation and the main functions on a small industry classification. The dimension packages timescales and geoscales apply the same functions to calendars and region hierarchies. The package website includes a roadmap of the package’s scope.

library(nestedscales)

Representation

A nested scale is a table with one row per leaf, the finest member of the dimension, and one column per frame, a resolution at which the leaves are grouped. The frames are given coarsest first. Numeric columns that are not frames are weights.

industries <- data.frame(
  section  = c("C", "C", "C", "D", "D"),
  division = c("C10", "C10", "C11", "D35", "D35"),
  class    = c("C101", "C102", "C110", "D351", "D352"),
  gva      = c(120, 80, 45, 300, 150)
)

ind <- scale_from_leaftable(
  industries,
  frames = c("section", "division", "class"),
  name   = "nace"
)
ind
#> NestedScale: nace
#> Frames (3, coarsest first):
#>   - section (2)
#>     - division (3)
#>       - class (5)
#> Leaves: 5
#> Weights: gva (default: gva)

The scale records the frames, the members at each frame, the leaf column and the weights:

scale_frames(ind)
#> [1] "section"  "division" "class"
scale_members(ind, "division")
#> [1] "C10" "C11" "D35"
scale_leaf_column(ind)
#> [1] "class"
scale_weights(ind)
#> [1] "gva"

Every frame partitions the leaves. Frames need not nest in each other: a member at one frame may belong to several members at a coarser frame, and two frames may be independent, in which case the leaves are their combinations. scale_nests(), scale_crosses() and scale_is_uniform() report the relation a given pair of frames has; no relation is assumed.

scale_nests(ind, "section", "division")
#> [1] TRUE
scale_family(ind, "section", "division")
#>   parent_frame parent child_frame child
#> 1      section      C    division   C10
#> 2      section      C    division   C11
#> 3      section      D    division   D35

Transition rules

Data keyed at one frame is converted to another frame with recast_scale(). Each value column follows a rule from SCALE_RULES:

rule aggregation (fine to coarse) disaggregation (coarse to fine)
sum sum split in proportion to the weight
weighted_mean weighted mean copy
mean mean over leaves copy
copy the common value copy
sd standard deviation over leaves not defined
share value as a share of its parent’s total not defined

The rule is given per value column, so extensive and intensive quantities convert in one call:

x <- data.frame(
  class = c("C101", "C102", "C110", "D351", "D352"),
  jobs  = c(12, 8, 5, 30, 20),
  wage  = c(31, 29, 27, 45, 40)
)

recast_scale(x, ind,
  source = "class", target = "section",
  rule = c(jobs = "sum", wage = "weighted_mean")
)
#>   section jobs     wage
#> 1       C   25 29.61224
#> 2       D   50 43.33333

The same function converts in the other direction. A total at the section frame is split over the classes in proportion to the weight:

y <- data.frame(section = c("C", "D"), investment = c(100, 400))

recast_scale(y, ind, source = "section", target = "class", rule = "sum")
#>   class investment
#> 1  C101   48.97959
#> 2  C102   32.65306
#> 3  C110   18.36735
#> 4  D351  266.66667
#> 5  D352  133.33333

Columns that are neither the key nor a value column are identifiers and are preserved as groups, so a panel of several years or scenarios converts in one call. A rule may also be registered once for a named value column with register_scale_rule(), after which rule = can be omitted for that column.

The same on time

Nothing above is specific to industries. Time is a dimension like any other: minutes group into hours and hours into days. The scale below is built from a table generated in code, two days of 24 hours of 60 minutes, with one row per minute. The codes of the hours and of the minutes include the day, so that every code names one member.

grid <- expand.grid(m = 0:59, h = 0:23, d = 1:2)
clock <- data.frame(
  day    = sprintf("d%d", grid$d),
  hour   = sprintf("d%d_h%02d", grid$d, grid$h),
  minute = sprintf("d%d_h%02d_m%02d", grid$d, grid$h, grid$m)
)
time <- scale_from_leaftable(clock, frames = c("day", "hour", "minute"),
                             name = "clock")
time
#> NestedScale: clock
#> Frames (3, coarsest first):
#>   - day (2)
#>     - hour (48)
#>       - minute (2880)
#> Leaves: 2880

A series recorded per minute is recast to hours and to days. A count, here the visitors entering a shop, is summed; a reading, here the temperature of the room, is averaged. Both series are invented.

series <- data.frame(
  minute   = clock$minute,
  visitors = grid$h %/% 6 + 1,
  temp     = 18 + grid$h / 4
)
head(series, 3)
#>       minute visitors temp
#> 1 d1_h00_m00        1   18
#> 2 d1_h00_m01        1   18
#> 3 d1_h00_m02        1   18

hourly <- recast_scale(series, time, source = "minute", target = "hour",
                       rule = c(visitors = "sum", temp = "mean"))
head(hourly, 3)
#>     hour visitors  temp
#> 1 d1_h00       60 18.00
#> 2 d1_h01       60 18.25
#> 3 d1_h02       60 18.50

recast_scale(series, time, source = "minute", target = "day",
             rule = c(visitors = "sum", temp = "mean"))
#>   day visitors   temp
#> 1  d1     3600 20.875
#> 2  d2     3600 20.875

The hourly table moves on in the same way, since hour is a frame like any other:

recast_scale(hourly[c("hour", "visitors")], time,
             source = "hour", target = "day", rule = "sum")
#>   day visitors
#> 1  d1     3600
#> 2  d2     3600

This example is only the bare mechanism: its minutes carry no dates, and every hour and every day has the same length. timescales builds on it for calendars with real dates, time zones, months of unequal length and typical or sampled periods.

Labels

join_scale() attaches the scale’s labels to a dataset: the member at the keyed frame, optionally the coarser frames (attach =) and the member’s share and weight (meta =):

join_scale(x, ind, frame = "class", attach = TRUE)
#>   class jobs wage nace.section nace.division nace
#> 1  C101   12   31            C           C10 C101
#> 2  C102    8   29            C           C10 C102
#> 3  C110    5   27            C           C11 C110
#> 4  D351   30   45            D           D35 D351
#> 5  D352   20   40            D           D35 D352

Subsets

filter_scale() keeps the leaves under given members; the result records what fraction of each weight it retains. prune_scale() collapses a scale to a coarser leaf frame.

manufacturing <- filter_scale(ind, "section", "C")
scale_members(manufacturing)
#> [1] "C101" "C102" "C110"
scale_coverage(manufacturing)
#>      gva 
#> 0.352518

scale_frames(prune_scale(ind, "division"))
#> [1] "section"  "division"

Attributes and aliases

A scale may carry values that belong to its members but are not weights: the persons per household of a city, a price per item, a wage per employee. They live in an attribute table keyed by (frame, member), at whatever frame they are published, and scale_attributes() resolves one value per member of a frame, walking to the nearest coarser frame when a member has none of its own. convert_scale() applies the resolved value row by row. Alternative names live in an alias table, and scale_match() resolves names against member names and aliases exactly, reporting ambiguity rather than guessing. A small scale of cities shows all three: seven cities in three regions in two countries, with a household size for region N1 and for city e, and a longer name for city a. The values are invented.

places <- scale_from_leaftable(
  data.frame(
    country = c("North", "North", "North", "North", "South", "South", "South"),
    region  = c("N1", "N1", "N2", "N2", "S1", "S1", "S1"),
    city    = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g")
  ),
  frames = c("country", "region", "city"), name = "places",
  attributes = data.frame(
    frame = c("region", "city"), member = c("N1", "e"),
    attribute = "hh_size", kind = "property", value = c(2.5, 2),
    unit_of_measure = "persons/household", source = "example"
  ),
  aliases = data.frame(frame = "city", member = "a", alias = "Alder",
                       source = "example")
)
scale_attributes(places, "hh_size", frame = "city")[
  c("member", "value", "unit_of_measure", "origin_frame")]
#>   member value   unit_of_measure origin_frame
#> 1      a   2.5 persons/household       region
#> 2      b   2.5 persons/household       region
#> 3      c    NA              <NA>         <NA>
#> 4      d    NA              <NA>         <NA>
#> 5      e   2.0 persons/household         city
#> 6      f    NA              <NA>         <NA>
#> 7      g    NA              <NA>         <NA>

people <- data.frame(city = c("a", "b", "e"), people = c(3, 2, 6))
convert_scale(people, places, "hh_size",
              from_unit = "persons", to_unit = "household")
#>   city people hh_size hh_size.origin_frame
#> 1    a    1.2     2.5               region
#> 2    b    0.8     2.5               region
#> 3    e    3.0     2.0                 city

scale_match(places, c("Alder", "B", "Zed"))
#>   label frame member method candidates
#> 1 Alder  city      a  alias       <NA>
#> 2     B  city      b  exact       <NA>
#> 3   Zed  <NA>   <NA>   none       <NA>

The cities a and b take the value of their region. The people are counted in thousands, so the converted column holds thousands of households.

vignette("attributes") has the full account.

Definition files

A scale is stored as a definition: a JSON header with its tables inline, or a bundle directory with Arrow or CSV tables, which the Python binding reads as well. write_scale() and read_scale() exchange them, and scale_catalog() lists the definitions installed packages ship:

path <- file.path(tempdir(), "nace.json")
write_scale(ind, path)
scale_frames(read_scale(path))
#> [1] "section"  "division" "class"
scale_catalog()[c("id", "name", "frames", "n_leaves", "package")]
#> [1] id       name     frames   n_leaves package 
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

Several dimensions

scale_product() combines scales into one multi-dimensional index without materialising the product of their leaves. recast_product(), join_product() and filter_product() apply the single-scale operations axis by axis.

p <- scale_product(a = scale_example(), b = scale_example2())
product_size(p)
#> $axes
#> a b 
#> 7 4 
#> 
#> $total
#> [1] 28

Further operations

  • cluster_scale() groups members by their data and returns the scale with the clusters as a new frame.
  • reconcile_scale() compares aggregated data with an independent total.
  • as_scale_array() converts long data to a dense array over a scale, and write_scale_dataset() stores data as an Arrow dataset together with its scales.

All operations accept a data.frame, tibble, data.table, dtplyr table or arrow dataset and return the same class; lazy inputs return a query unless collect = TRUE.
